subject: Physics
scope: 20 original AQA Physics 7408 Year 1 Mechanics and Materials mock recall items.
notes: Chosen after checking pre-existing cards and 3.4.1.1–3.4.2.2 left-column requirements. Focuses on direction/sign errors, conceptual questions and practical interpretation. Does NOT certify full mock coverage. Does not alter earlier progress, IDs or school Maths mock scope.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Two perpendicular vector components have magnitudes P and Q. What is the magnitude of the resultant?
cards.back: √(P² + Q²).
accept: √(P² + Q²).
Square root of P squared plus Q squared.
Use Pythagoras on the perpendicular components.
reject: P + Q always.
PQ.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For horizontal Fx>0 and vertical Fy, what is the resultant angle θ above the horizontal?
cards.back: tan θ = Fy/Fx (choose the correct quadrant if a component is negative).
accept: tan θ = Fy/Fx (choose the correct quadrant if a component is negative).
theta equals arctan of vertical component divided by horizontal component, with direction checked.
Use the inverse tangent of Fy divided by Fx and check signs.
reject: tan theta = Fx/Fy always.
Only the resultant magnitude gives its direction.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: If three forces acting at one point form a closed head-to-tail vector triangle, what is their resultant?
cards.back: Zero; the forces are in equilibrium.
accept: Zero; the forces are in equilibrium.
The vector sum is zero.
Resultant force equals zero.
reject: Their resultant must equal the largest force.
The forces necessarily cause acceleration.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: A force F acts at angle θ to a lever arm of length r. What is its moment magnitude about the pivot?
cards.back: Fr sin θ.
accept: Fr sin θ.
Force times the perpendicular distance to its line of action.
M = F r sin(theta).
reject: Fr cos θ for any angle.
Always Fr even if the force points at the pivot.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why is it useful to take moments about the point where an unknown reaction force acts?
cards.back: Its perpendicular distance from the pivot is zero, so it contributes zero moment.
accept: Its perpendicular distance from the pivot is zero, so it contributes zero moment.
The reaction force then has no moment about that pivot.
Its line of action passes through the chosen pivot, eliminating its moment.
reject: It eliminates the force from the vertical force balance too.
The reaction force itself becomes zero.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: An object has positive velocity but negative acceleration. Is it necessarily moving backwards?
cards.back: No; it is still moving forwards but its speed is decreasing while those signs persist.
accept: No; it is still moving forwards but its speed is decreasing while those signs persist.
It travels in the positive direction and slows down.
Negative acceleration alone does not mean negative velocity.
reject: Yes, negative acceleration always means backwards motion.
Its velocity must already be negative.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does a negative signed area under an acceleration–time graph tell you?
cards.back: Velocity has decreased algebraically over that interval; it does not by itself show negative velocity.
accept: Velocity has decreased algebraically over that interval; it does not by itself show negative velocity.
There is a negative change in velocity.
Delta v is negative, not necessarily v.
reject: Distance travelled is negative.
The object must be travelling backwards for the whole interval.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Free fall from rest, downward positive, drag negligible: velocity–time graph gradient?
cards.back: +g, approximately 9.81 m s⁻².
accept: +g, approximately 9.81 m s⁻².
The gradient is g.
Positive gravitational acceleration, about 9.81 metres per second squared.
reject: Zero, because it starts at rest.
Negative g when downward has been defined as positive.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: At the highest point of an ideal projectile's flight, what are its vertical velocity and vertical acceleration?
cards.back: Vertical velocity is zero; vertical acceleration remains g downwards.
accept: Vertical velocity is zero; vertical acceleration remains g downwards.
Vy = 0 and ay = -g if upwards is positive.
Its vertical velocity is instantaneously zero but acceleration is still downward at 9.81 metres per second squared.
reject: Both vertical velocity and vertical acceleration are zero.
Vertical acceleration changes to upwards at the top.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Same projectile launch speed and angle: how does air resistance affect horizontal range?
cards.back: The horizontal range is reduced.
accept: The horizontal range is reduced.
It travels a shorter horizontal distance.
Air resistance generally reduces the range.
reject: It always travels further horizontally.
Air resistance has no effect on the trajectory.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For a falling object reaching terminal speed, how do upward air resistance and downward weight compare?
cards.back: They are equal in magnitude, so the resultant force and acceleration are zero.
accept: They are equal in magnitude, so the resultant force and acceleration are zero.
Drag equals weight at terminal speed.
Upward resistive force balances mg.
reject: Weight is larger than drag at terminal speed.
Drag must vanish when terminal speed is reached.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: A book rests on a table. Is the table's normal force the Newton's-third-law partner of the book's weight?
cards.back: No; weight and normal force act on the same book, whereas a third-law pair acts on different objects.
accept: No; weight and normal force act on the same book, whereas a third-law pair acts on different objects.
No. The reaction to Earth's pull on the book is the book's gravitational pull on Earth.
No, normal contact force and weight can balance but are not an action-reaction pair.
reject: Yes, because they are equal and opposite forces on the book.
Yes, because any balanced forces form a third-law pair.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why must velocities, rather than unsigned speeds, be used when conserving momentum in one dimension?
cards.back: Momentum is a vector, so opposite directions must have opposite signs.
accept: Momentum is a vector, so opposite directions must have opposite signs.
Velocity has direction and signed momenta must be added.
Conservation of momentum needs positive and negative directions.
reject: Momentum has no direction.
All velocities should be made positive before adding momentum.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What distinguishes an elastic collision from an inelastic collision when the system is isolated?
cards.back: Total kinetic energy is conserved in an elastic collision; total momentum is conserved in both.
accept: Total kinetic energy is conserved in an elastic collision; total momentum is conserved in both.
Elastic collisions conserve kinetic energy as well as momentum.
Momentum is conserved in both, but kinetic energy is not generally conserved in an inelastic collision.
reject: Only elastic collisions conserve momentum.
Inelastic collisions conserve total kinetic energy by definition.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: On a force–displacement graph, how do you find net work done by a force that changes sign?
cards.back: Add the signed areas between the force curve and displacement axis.
accept: Add the signed areas between the force curve and displacement axis.
Work equals positive area minus the magnitudes of negative areas.
Integrate force with respect to displacement, retaining signs.
reject: Add the absolute values of every area.
Use the gradient of the force-displacement graph.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: When a moving object stops because of friction, where does its initial kinetic energy mainly go?
cards.back: It is transferred to thermal internal energy of the object and surroundings.
accept: It is transferred to thermal internal energy of the object and surroundings.
Work against friction increases internal energy.
Kinetic energy is dissipated as heating.
reject: Energy is destroyed.
Kinetic energy must become gravitational potential energy.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Can a material stop obeying Hooke's law yet still return to its original length when unloaded?
cards.back: Yes; the limit of proportionality and the elastic limit are not necessarily the same.
accept: Yes; the limit of proportionality and the elastic limit are not necessarily the same.
Yes, nonlinear elastic behaviour is possible before plastic deformation.
The force-extension graph may become nonlinear without permanent extension.
reject: No, any nonlinearity must cause permanent deformation.
The elastic limit must always coincide with the limit of proportionality.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Same material and wire length; diameter doubles. How does axial stiffness change in elastic region?
cards.back: It becomes four times as large because cross-sectional area is proportional to diameter squared.
accept: It becomes four times as large because cross-sectional area is proportional to diameter squared.
Stiffness quadruples.
k is four times the original because A is four times larger.
reject: Stiffness doubles.
Stiffness halves.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does a non-zero positive extension remaining after a wire is unloaded show?
cards.back: Plastic deformation has occurred.
accept: Plastic deformation has occurred.
The wire has a permanent extension.
The material has gone beyond its elastic limit.
reject: The wire was perfectly elastic.
It proves Hooke's law held throughout loading.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why should a micrometer's zero error be checked when measuring wire diameter for Young modulus?
cards.back: A systematic zero offset biases the diameter, hence the calculated area and Young modulus.
accept: A systematic zero offset biases the diameter, hence the calculated area and Young modulus.
Zero error introduces systematic diameter error, which affects area squared in diameter.
The micrometer may read nonzero when closed and all diameters need correction.
reject: Zero error is removed by taking more readings alone.
Wire diameter does not affect Young modulus calculations.
